title: A Day With No Hellos
concept: After this one you can tell a warm nod from a cold one, and you can feel what a day with almost none costs you.
bookIdea: Any sign that someone registers you, from a greeting to a glare, and people need a steady supply of them to stay well.
bookSource: Games People Play, Introduction; Scripts People Live, ch. 1

opener.setting: Monday, 7:50am. Hawthorn Court, apartment 3B, the kitchen. You moved in two days ago.

lines.cue: headphones in, pouring cereal, not looking up

lines.text: “Morning.”

opener.ask: Nothing bad has happened yet, so why does the day already feel like it is draining you?

rounds.label: Spot, round 1
rounds.intro: Each card is one line from today. Tap what it was: a warm nod, a cold nod, or nothing at all.

items.cue: 9:35. She looks at her screen, not at you, and prints the badge.
items.why: A cold nod still counts. She said one word and printed your badge, so she registered that you exist. Cold nods are still food.

traps.0: A warm nod would mean she was glad you came. Her eyes never left the screen, so calling it warm has you waiting for a smile that won't come.
traps.2: Nothing would mean she never noticed you. She did, and the day starts draining from this desk.

items.example:
A school gate, 8:10am.
Teacher: “Name?”
She ticks the list and says “Sit” without lifting her head.
The child goes in. That is a nod, even a thin one, because the teacher saw the child.

items.text: “Oh, new boy! You're too thin. Come, come, I've made flattened rice.”
items.why: A warm nod can sound like a complaint. Gran says you're too thin because she cares whether you eat. The complaint is the affection.

traps.1: A cold nod would need her to be annoyed with you. She is delighted, and she is already holding out the flattened rice.
traps.2: Nothing would mean she never saw you. She stood in her doorway and called you in.

items.example:
A family WhatsApp group.
Uncle: “You look tired, eat something.”
It reads like a telling-off, but it is the same worry that makes him ask about your day.

items.cue: You say 'Morning' to his back. He nods at the cereal without turning round.
items.why: A cold nod. It was small and it went to the cereal, but it still tells you he knows you are in the kitchen. That is more than nothing.

traps.0: A warm nod needs him to turn round and look at you. He stays facing the cereal, so calling it warm would be a guess.
traps.2: Nothing would mean you were invisible in that kitchen. He did nod, and a nod counts, even a small one.

items.example:
A bus stop, 7:40am.
You say “Morning” to the back of a man's head.
He lifts two fingers off the rail without turning round.

items.text: “Oh thank god, someone newer than me.”
items.cue: canteen, 13:10, after you ask if you can sit down
items.why: A warm nod for being there. She's glad you came, and you didn't have to do anything to earn it.

traps.1: A cold nod would mean she wanted you gone. She is relieved, and cold gets her wrong.
traps.2: Nothing would mean she didn't hear you. She looked up from her phone the moment you spoke.

items.example:
A family lunch.
Cousin: “Oh good, you came, the kids kept asking for you.”
That is warm, and it is for being there, not for anything you did.

items.why: A warm nod. The question sounds like a checklist, but it means she has you in mind when you're not there. Even a worried question is a nod for being.

traps.1: A cold nod would make her a nag. She asks because she misses you, so cold reads her too harshly.
traps.2: Nothing would mean no word from home at all. A question about your dinner is still her looking after you.

items.example:
A neighbour's balcony, evening.
“You're back late. Have you eaten?”
It can feel like a checklist. It is also a sign she noticed you were out.

rounds.label: Play, the day in motion
rounds.intro: The day, then the walk home. Each beat gives you two or three things to say. Watch the You meter. It drains whenever nobody notices you.

items.title: Monday, 7:50 to 22:30
items.setting: Six places in one day: the flat, the stairwell, Halden reception, Daniel's desk, the canteen and your room. The You meter starts at 70.

lines.text: “Morning.” You say it to his back.
lines.outcome: He nods at the cereal.
lines.why: A hello aimed at someone's back is too small to land. It counts as a nod, but he barely took it in, so the morning starts thin.

lines.text: You tap his shoulder. “Hey, I'm the new guy in the back room. We haven't actually met.”
lines.outcome: He pulls out one earbud. “Oh, yeah! Sam. Sorry, mornings.”
lines.why: You gave him a reason to look up. Saying who you are is the simplest way to get a nod that actually lands.

lines.text: Say nothing and make tea.
lines.outcome: The kettle is the loudest thing in the room.
lines.why: Going quiet so you can't be turned away is the most expensive move of the morning. You gave up a chance to be seen, and the kettle filled the gap.

beats.text: “Oh, new boy! You're too thin. Come, come, I've made flattened rice.”
beats.cue: stairwell, 8:15, her door open. You have twenty minutes to make the bus.

lines.text: “I'm late, Gran, sorry!” (keep walking)
lines.outcome: Her door stays open, but her smile goes. “Late, late, always late,” she tells the stairs.
lines.why: Walking past a warm nod in a hurry lands as a cold one. You were polite about the bus, but she heard only that the flattened rice could wait.

lines.text: Stop at the door. “I can't today, but I'd love to on Saturday. Keep some for me?”
lines.outcome: “Saturday it is. And eat something!”
lines.why: You said no to today and yes to Saturday, so she still gets to feed you. A no that comes with a yes keeps the nod flowing.

lines.text: Go in and eat. Miss the bus and arrive 25 minutes late.
lines.outcome: Her kitchen smells of ginger, and the bus leaves without you. You reach Halden 25 minutes late.
lines.why: The warm nod was real, and it cost you your own time. Keep that in mind, because the cost comes back later in the week.

beats.cue: 9:35. No eye contact. The screen takes most of her attention.

lines.text: “Thanks. Fourth floor, got it.”
lines.outcome: Her eyes flick up for a second. Nothing else, but a second is something.
lines.why: Thanking her costs nothing and gets a flicker back. The drain still happens here, because you can't pull a nod out of a screen.

lines.text: Take the badge in silence.
lines.outcome: The badge goes on the lanyard. Four more points gone without a word.
lines.why: Taking the badge without a word is what almost everyone does. It keeps the desk moving and leaves you a little lower.

beats.text: “You're the new backend hire. Good. Omar will show you the repo. Standup's at ten, don't be late to it, I hate that.”
beats.cue: not standing, not looking up. If you came in late, he adds “…and you already were.”

lines.text: “Got it.”
lines.outcome: He's already back on his screen.
lines.why: Got it is correct and flat. Nothing is offered back, so nothing comes back.

lines.text: “Thanks, I'm looking forward to it. Anything you want me to read before standup?”
lines.outcome: He looks up, surprised. “…The incident log. Nobody reads it.”
lines.why: Asking for something he knows about gives him a chance to be the expert, and that earns a real answer.

lines.text: “Sorry, sorry, won't happen again.” (said whether or not you were late)
lines.outcome: He frowns. “Won't what happen?”
lines.why: Saying sorry for nothing hands him a fault he never named. He frowns because he doesn't know what you mean.

beats.cue: canteen, 13:10. Six tables. Clara is alone at one, laughing at her phone. The others are full of people who already know each other.

lines.text: Sit alone and eat fast.
lines.outcome: You finish in twelve minutes, and nobody asks where you went.
lines.why: Eating alone with a free seat in view is a way of not being looked at. It feels safe, and it is the same as being invisible.

lines.text: “Mind if I? I don't know anyone yet.”
lines.outcome: “Oh thank god, someone newer than me.” She looks up for the first time.
lines.why: Admitting you're new is a small, true thing to say, and it gets a warm nod back.

lines.text: Join the big table without asking.
lines.outcome: Two people shift along to make room. Nobody introduces themselves.
lines.why: Sitting down without a word puts you in a conversation you weren't asked into. Everyone makes room, and nobody makes you welcome.

beats.text: “Did you eat? Your father says you should have taken the offer from the other city. I told him you know what you're doing. Did you eat?”
beats.cue: phone, your room, 22:30, the door shut

lines.text: “I ate, Mum. It was a long day. I'm fine.”
lines.outcome: “Fine, fine. Everyone's fine. Sleep.” The call ends in forty seconds.
lines.why: The answer is true and closes the door. She got a report, not a conversation, so the nod doesn't land.

lines.text: “The truth is, nobody really talked to me today. It was weird.”
lines.outcome: A pause. “…First days are like that. Your father's first day at the mill, he came home and sat on the step for an hour.”
lines.why: Saying the true thing gets the first real nod of the day. It is small and late, but it reaches her.

lines.text: “Mum, I'm 27. You don't have to ask if I ate every day.”
lines.outcome: “I'll stop asking, then.”
lines.why: That line may be true, but it shuts the door. She loses the one thing she can still do from far away, and you lose a nod.

fallout.you: You run out. You eat standing up and skip the call, and the day closes on an empty screen.

items.example:
A new hostel in a new city.
Day one, the warden says hello and asks your name. By day ten the corridor has stopped looking up.

items.title: Monday, 18:05, the way home
items.setting: The day is nearly over, and four people stand between Halden and your bed. Each of them has a nod to spare if you give them a reason. The You meter starts at 50.

beats.cue: 18:05. Same woman, same flat voice, coat half on. This time she looks up at you.

lines.text: “Night. Thanks for sorting my badge this morning.”
lines.outcome: A short laugh. “Mind the lift on four, it sticks.”
lines.why: Naming one thing she did tells her it was seen. A nod you hand over tends to come back, and hers is warmer than the one she gave you at 9:35.

lines.text: “Night.”
lines.outcome: The door swings shut behind her. Even, and no more.
lines.why: You matched her word for word. A matched hello keeps things square and adds nothing.

lines.text: Look at your phone and walk past.
lines.outcome: She says it again, to your back and a little flatter. “Night.”
lines.why: She gave you a nod and got none back. People notice that straight away.

beats.text: “Repo's a mess, right? Everyone says sorry on day one.”
beats.cue: 18:20, by the lift on four, bag on one shoulder, grinning at his phone.

lines.text: “It is. I lost an hour in the build folder. Is it always like that?”
lines.outcome: He pockets the phone. “Always. I'll draw you a map tomorrow.”
lines.why: You told him one small true thing and asked for his help. Admitting you struggled gives him a nod to hand over, and he hands it over.

lines.text: “Yeah, a bit.”
lines.outcome: He nods. The lift comes, and you ride down watching the floor numbers.
lines.why: True and flat. Nothing gets offered, so nothing comes back.

lines.text: “I think I got everything wrong today.”
lines.outcome: “You didn't. Stop it.” He means it kindly, and it is over in a breath.
lines.why: Fishing for comfort gets a quick, polite answer. It is a nod, though a thin one, and he only gave it because you asked.

beats.text: “Oh. Hey. Sorry about this morning, I'm not a person before ten.”
beats.cue: 3B kitchen, 19:10. Noodles in the pan, headphones round his neck for once.

lines.text: “No worries. Is there anything about this flat I should know?”
lines.outcome: He puts the fork down. “Yeah. Don't use the blue towel. And the boiler hates Mondays.”
lines.why: Asking for something only he knows gives him a nod to give, and he gives you more than you asked for.

lines.text: “Don't worry about it.”
lines.outcome: “Cool.” He goes back to the noodles.
lines.why: Kind, and it closes the topic. The nod you gave him was real, and the one you got back is tiny.

lines.text: Take your tea to your room without a word.
lines.outcome: Your door clicks. A moment later you hear his headphones go back on.
lines.why: Slipping away protects you from a cold reply, and it costs you the warm one he was holding out. It is the biggest drain of the evening.

beats.text: “You haven't forgotten Saturday, have you? Eleven o'clock.”
beats.cue: 3B front door, 20:30. She has climbed the stairs with a covered plate.

lines.text: “Eleven on Saturday. I wrote it on my hand.” (hold it up)
lines.outcome: She laughs and presses the plate into your hands. “Eat it hot!”
lines.why: A small proof that you listened is worth more to her than a promise. It earns the warmest nod of the evening, and a hot dinner.

lines.text: “I'll try to make it.”
lines.outcome: “Try, try.” She sets the plate on the table, and the smile stays on her mouth only.
lines.why: A hedge in answer to a warm invitation reads as cold. She asked for a yes and got a maybe.

lines.text: “Gran, you really don't have to feed me.”
lines.outcome: “Of course I don't have to,” she says, and the plate is on the table before you finish.
lines.why: Waving off a warm nod tells her it was not wanted. She keeps giving, and you take less than she gave.

items.example:
A shared lift at the end of a long shift.
“Night!” “Night. Thanks for covering the desk.”
Two short lines, and both people walk out lighter.

items.text: Nothing bad happened all day, and you still ran out of steam by night. What explains it?
options: You were late, and everyone was cross with you
Few people gave you nods, and a person runs low without them
You talked too much on the bus and tired yourself out
items.why: Being noticed is a need. Most of the day had nothing for you, and cold nods still counted. A day with almost none drains you the way a day without food does.

traps.0: Lateness explains one bad moment, but nobody was angry with you all day. Blaming it would have you apologising to everyone, which is one more drain.
traps.2: Talking on the bus is a guess with no evidence behind it. You barely talked to anyone all day, and that is the problem.

items.example:
A class reunion, a week later.
Two old classmates say hello and go back to their drinks.
You drive home tired. Nobody was rude, and nobody looked for you either.

debrief.nadia: Being noticed is food. A day without it drains you the way a day without food does. Daniel's “don't be late” counted, and so did the receptionist saying “Name?”. Cold nods are still food, so count them too.
debrief.bookNote: The books call this a stroke: any sign that someone noticed you exist, from a hello to a glare, and people need a steady supply of them to stay well.

reflection.prompt: Think about the last week. Which person noticed you most, and did you let them?
